headline: A THOUSAND DOLLARS BOUGHT 32.4 MILLION VIEWS FOR ONE SONG, BECAUSE THE PAYOUTS WERE CAPPED.  AT THE PUBLISHED RATE THAT SHOULD HAVE COST THIRTY TIMES MORE
deck: Twitch's chief executive spent last week publicly embracing the clip economy, and Tubefilter asked yesterday whether clips are why the platform's viewership is up.  Nobody has proved that.  But underneath the question sits a distribution market with a published rate card, and almost nobody on the brand side has read it properly.
tldr: One clipping campaign for John Summit's Lights Go Out had an initial budget of 1,050 dollars and produced 32.4 million views across 29 clips from 13 creators, because clipper payouts are capped while a clip's reach is not.  Budget clipping as a bounded number of attempts rather than views multiplied by a rate, and run one capped test on long-form you already own.

The clips that carried that campaign put the song underneath footage people already wanted to watch, so the viewer received the product in three seconds rather than a signpost to it.  Before you commission any clip, check that the fragment itself delivers the thing you are selling, and if it only points at it, spend the money elsewhere.

Cakes Body has done 100 million dollars a year for two years and says its most viral content for three running years has been mission-driven and completely unrelated to product.  Count how many of your twenty best organic posts actually feature the product, and take that ratio into your next planning meeting as the baseline.

Converse never named who approved its pulled ad, and for nearly a week Grok and Google both named a chief marketing officer who had left the company in January, who then received threats and had his family doxxed.  Query the answer engines for who runs marketing at your brand before your next crisis statement goes out, and put the correct name in the statement.

EA Sports FC 27 peaked at 444,700 concurrent viewers over ten days and sponsored broadcasts produced 2.33 percent of its hours watched, which Streams Charts calls typical for a major launch.  Ask any launch sponsorship seller what share of hours came from paid broadcasts on the last comparable title before you price the deal.

Kick took 43.6 percent of that game's hours watched against Twitch's 48.9, on a title where Twitch normally leads by far more.  Put Kick on your next livestream plan as a named line with its own brand-safety position agreed in advance, rather than leaving it off by default.

YouTube is extending live reaction to long-form video, with the reacting creator keeping the ad revenue and the original creator getting attribution and undefined view credit.  Get the list of your brand videos carrying paid integrations and ask your YouTube representative whether brand channels are opted in by default and where the per-video control sits.

**A THOUSAND DOLLARS BOUGHT 32.4 MILLION VIEWS FOR ONE SONG, BECAUSE THE PAYOUTS WERE CAPPED.  AT THE PUBLISHED RATE THAT SHOULD HAVE COST THIRTY TIMES MORE**
Twitch's chief executive spent last week publicly embracing the clip economy, and Tubefilter asked yesterday whether clips are why the platform's viewership is up.  Nobody has proved that.  But underneath the question sits a distribution market with a published rate card, and almost nobody on the brand side has read it properly.

**1.** One clipping campaign for John Summit's Lights Go Out had an initial budget of 1,050 dollars and produced 32.4 million views across 29 clips from 13 creators, because clipper payouts are capped while a clip's reach is not.  Budget clipping as a bounded number of attempts rather than views multiplied by a rate, and run one capped test on long-form you already own.

Before you commission any clip, check that the fragment itself delivers the thing you are selling, and if it only points at it, spend the money elsewhere.

Ask any launch sponsorship seller what share of hours came from paid broadcasts on the last comparable title before you price the deal.
**6.** Kick took 43.6 percent of that game's hours watched against Twitch's 48.9, on a title where Twitch normally leads by far more.  Put Kick on your next livestream plan as a named line with its own brand-safety position agreed in advance, rather than leaving it off by default.
